1.pericope_label: Now those that sealed were, Nehemiah, the Tirshatha, the son of Hachaliah, and Zidkijah, Seraiah, Azariah, Jeremiah, Pashur, Amariah, Malchijah,

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch fix the sense of the opening words against two older readings: the phrase means upon all this, on the foundation of the preceding prayer and penitence, and not after all this, nor in all the evil that had befallen us as Rashi and Aben Ezra took it; the word for what was made is a settlement or sure agreement rather than a covenant in the sacrificial sense. On the Levitical names they keep to the record, that fourteen Levites sealed, that the sons of two of them had returned with Zerubbabel among seventy-four others, that four of the names occur elsewhere as heads of orders, and that of the rest nothing further is known though they may be regarded as heads of Levitical houses. Ellicott works by identification: the first name on the list is the family name of the high-priestly house to which both Ezra and Eliashib belonged, so that one of them, probably Ezra, affixed its seal, and another of the names he takes for Zadok the scribe, who was Nehemiah's secretary.
Gill says only that these are they who sealed the covenant, and leaves the identifications and the arithmetic to the others.

Clarke sets out the order of subscription in four classes, Nehemiah first as governor, then the priests, then the Levites, then the chiefs of the people, and finds it strange that neither Ezra nor the high priest Eliashib nor any of the prophets appears, though some of the prophets must have been at Jerusalem. He closes with a textual note the others do not raise, that the whole of this chapter except its first two verses is wanting in the Arabic version. Wesley reads the sealing as done both in the subscribers' own names and in the name of all the rest, and proposes an impediment for Ezra, sickness or something like it, supporting the guess from the later narrative where Ezra reappears at the dedication of the wall.

Henry begins with the change in the form of covenanting, that when Israel was first brought into covenant it was by sacrifice and the sprinkling of blood, while here it is by the more natural and common way of sealing and subscribing written articles which bound the people to no more than was already their duty. He counts the subscribers, twenty-two priests, seventeen Levites and forty-four of the chief of the people, and draws his lesson from the order rather than the numbers, that those above others in dignity and power should go before them in the way of God. He observes that the Levites who subscribed included those who had been the mouth of the congregation in prayer, which showed them affected by what they had said and unwilling to bind burdens on others that they declined to touch; and that most of those named earlier as heads of houses appear here among the first of the chief of the people, the present head bearing the name of him who was head when they came out of Babylon. On Ezra's absence he supposes that, having already done his part as a scribe, he left it to others to do theirs.

debates.question: Why is Ezra not among those who sealed?

positions.position: Having already done his part as a scribe, he left this part to others
Unexplained and strange, and the difficulty is wider, since Eliashib and the prophets are missing too
Hindered by sickness or some like impediment, from which he was free by the dedication of the wall
He is there: the first name is his high-priestly family name, and probably Ezra himself affixed its seal

outliers.claim: Notes that the whole of this chapter except its first two verses is wanting in the Arabic version, a textual observation no other voice raises.
Observes that the Levites who subscribed were those who had been the mouth of the congregation in prayer, so that they would not bind burdens on others which they themselves declined to touch.

themes: Now those that sealed were, Nehemiah, the Tirshatha, the son of Hachaliah, and Zidkijah,

8.pericope_label: Maaziah, Bilgai, Shemaiah: these were the priests. And the Levites: both Jeshua the son of Azaniah, Binnui of the sons of Henadad, Kadmiel;

schools.summary: Ellicott is the only voice on these two verses and his notes are short. On the first he observes that what the text calls the priests means the names of the priestly families rather than of individual men, referring the reader to the fuller priestly list given later in this book. On the second he reports only how far the names can be checked, that five of the Levitical family names are traceable in the earlier registers of the return and in the list of those who came up with Ezra. He offers no identification of the remaining names, no account of why these particular houses sealed, and no comment on the order in which they stand.

outliers.claim: Establishes that the signatories of both orders sign as houses rather than as individuals, and that a minority of the Levitical houses can be matched against registers already in hand.

themes: Maaziah, Bilgai, Shemaiah: these were the priests.
And the Levites: both Jeshua the son of Azaniah, Binnui of the sons of Henadad, Kadmiel;

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch treat the roll of the chief of the people as a document to be checked against another document. Forty-four names stand under the heading; thirteen are found in the register of the kindreds who returned with Zerubbabel, and the remaining thirty-one are accounted for as heads of the particular houses into which those larger kindreds were divided, or as elders of the smaller towns of Benjamin and Judah which had no kindred name to sign under. The arithmetic between the two lists does not resolve in one direction: the earlier register carries thirty-three kindreds and places against forty-four here, but several names standing there are missing here, so the later roll is both longer and in places different rather than the earlier roll with names appended. Two causes are offered and neither is made to carry the difference alone, that a kindred included several houses whose heads each subscribed separately, and that the number of houses had itself grown over the intervening years. They do not apportion the increase between the two causes, nor explain the names that have dropped out.

outliers.claim: Establish that the roll is a list of signing units rather than of kindreds, so that it cannot be set against the earlier register name for name and a difference in length carries no conclusion about how many families had returned.

14.pericope_label: The chief of the people; Parosh, Pahath–moab, Elam, Zatthu, Bani,

schools.summary: Ellicott is again the only commentator, and his note is about the kind of list this is rather than about any name in it. The heading covers a mixture: some of the names are personal, some belong to families, some represent places, and some stand independent of any of these, so that the list can be read neither as a roll of individuals nor as a roll of clans. His second observation is comparative, that setting this catalogue beside the register of those who returned from the captivity shows the years between to have added to the number of houses. The growth is left as an observation rather than pressed into an argument, with no figure given and no account of whether it came from natural increase, from the subdivision of older kindreds, or from families joining the community after the return.

outliers.claim: Notes that the heading covers personal names, family names, place names and independent names together, so the catalogue cannot be read consistently as either a roll of persons or a roll of clans.

themes: The chief of the people; Parosh, Pahath–moab, Elam, Zatthu, Bani,

28.pericope_label: And the rest of the people, the priests, the Levites, the porters, the singers, the Nethinims, and all they that had separated themselves from the people of the lands unto the law of God, their wives, their sons, and their daughters, every one having knowledge, and having understanding; They clave to their brethren, their nobles, and entered into a curse, and into an oath, to walk in God’s law, which was given by Moses the servant of God, and to observe and do all the commandments of the Lord our Lord, and his judgments and his statutes; And that we would not give our daughters unto the people of the land, nor take their daughters for our sons: And if the people of the land bring ware or any victuals on the sabbath day to sell, that we would not buy it of them on the sabbath, or on the holy day: and that we would leave the seventh year, and the exaction of every debt.

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch define the rest of the people as the members of the community exclusive of the princes and the heads of the priestly and Levitical orders, and suppose the Nethinim, among whom they count the servants of Solomon, to have been represented by the heads of the Levites. Those who had separated themselves they identify as the descendants of the Israelites left in the land who were now joining the new community, and they read the construction as significant, since the separation is not merely from the peoples but toward the law of God, which is to say in order to live by it. Ellicott refuses the natural reading of that clause on three grounds: there is as yet no record of a recognised body of converts from heathenism, the word for separated stands elsewhere in this book with another sense, and the following verses show the covenant concerned precisely with the danger arising out of commerce with the heathen. He adds that children able to take the oath intelligently were included, calls the people's act a union springing from a deep national conviction, and distinguishes the two instruments exactly, the oath assuming the obligation and the curse imprecating the penalty of violation. On the sabbath he extends the prohibition to the great festivals equally with the weekly rest, takes the sabbatical year as following naturally with the ground left untilled, and identifies the last clause with the release of debts belonging to that year.

Gill takes the rest of the people for those who did not themselves sign and seal, and has them declaring their approbation and ratifying what had been done in their name. On the marriage clause he reads it against the history, that they had intermarried already, were prone to it, and did it again after this; and he glosses the word for ware as anything that could be sold and carried away.

Clarke turns the representation into a claim, that every one of the rest had his representative in one or another of the classes that sealed and was bound by their sealing, and observes that although they did not sign the instrument they bound themselves by a solemn oath to fulfil its conditions; the marriage clause he reduces to a phrase, that they would make no affinity with the people of the land, and the sabbath clause to two resolutions, that the sabbath should be kept and the land have its own rest every seventh year. Wesley presses the social point hardest, that the commonalty agreed with their nobles, that great men never look so great as when they encourage religion and are examples of it, and that the nobles are here called their brethren since in the things of God rich and poor meet together; on the sabbath he adds the reason for singling out that commandment, since its profanation is a sure inlet to all manner of profaneness.

debates.question: Who are they that had separated themselves from the people of the lands?

positions.position: Not converts from heathenism: no such recognised body is yet on record, the word bears another sense elsewhere in this book, and the covenant is aimed at the danger of commerce with the heathen
The descendants of the Israelites left in the land, now joining the new community, separated toward the law of God in order to live by it

outliers.claim: Holds that great men never look so great as when they encourage religion and are examples of it, nor can they secure the regard of the best of their inferiors by anything more surely.
Separates the two instruments precisely, the oath assuming the obligation and the curse imprecating the penalty of its violation.

themes: And the rest of the people, the priests, the Levites, the porters, the singers, the Nethinims, and all they that had separated themselves from the people of the lands unto the law of God, their wives, their sons, and their daughters, every one having knowledge, and having understanding;

They clave to their brethren, their nobles, and entered into a curse, and into an oath, to walk in God’s law, which was given by Moses the servant of God, and to observe and do all the commandments of the Lord our Lord, and his judgments and his statutes;

32.pericope_label: Also we made ordinances for us, to charge ourselves yearly with the third part of a shekel for the service of the house of our God; For the shewbread, and for the continual meat offering, and for the continual burnt offering, of the sabbaths, of the new moons, for the set feasts, and for the holy things, and for the sin offerings to make an atonement for Israel, and for all the work of the house of our God. And we cast the lots among the priests, the Levites, and the people, for the wood offering, to bring it into the house of our God, after the houses of our fathers, at times appointed year by year, to burn upon the altar of the Lord our God, as it is written in the law:

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch treat the payment as a revival of the Mosaic precept that every man of twenty years and upwards should give half a shekel, a tribute still being paid in the gospel period, with the rate alone altered, lowered to a third in consideration of the poverty of the greater part of the community; they reject Aben Ezra's view that the third was an addition to the half rather than a reduction of it as unsupported by the text, note that the text does not say who was liable and take this as evidence that the custom was already well known, and restrict the term for service to the regular worship rather than the building and repair of the temple. On the wood they state the gap in the law exactly, that it prescribes fire to be kept burning and wood to be burnt every morning but gives no direction about procuring it, so that the rulers must always have made some arrangement. Ellicott finds in the arrangement the origin of the feast of the wood offering, a single day afterwards substituted for the appointed times through the year, and adds that the lot determined the order in which the classes supplied it.

Gill notices first what kind of thing this is, an ordinance the people made among themselves binding them to what the law of God had not bound them to. On the wood he notes only how the lot was drawn, the priests and Levites together in one and the people in another.

Clarke supplies the historical reason why an arrangement for the wood was needed now. Fetching it had been the business of the Nethinim, the hewers of wood and drawers of water, and after the captivity few of them were to be found, since as descendants of the Gibeonites they were reckoned little better than slaves and had as much interest in staying where they were as in returning. With too few left, the lot was cast, and he is precise that it did not decide who should furnish the wood but which class or district should furnish it at which season, so that the supply should be continuous. He reports that the bringing of the wood afterwards grew into a great day and was constituted a feast, which Josephus names as the carrying of the wood, and remarks that it is absent from the sacred writings because while the Nethinim were numerous there was no occasion for it.

Henry approaches the fund from the side of necessity. There had formerly been treasures in the house of the Lord for this charge and they were gone, with no settled fund in their place; the table and altar were a constant expense, they had no rich king to provide as Hezekiah had, and the priests' own maintenance was too small to bear it. So the people charged themselves, and he makes the arithmetic the moral, that when every one will act and every one will give, though but little, the whole amount will be considerable. He is careful to add that the governor did not impose the tax but that the people made it an ordinance for themselves.

debates.question: Is the third of a shekel a new ordinance or an altered old one?

positions.position: New: an ordinance the people made among themselves, binding them to what the law of God had not
Old: a revival of the Mosaic half-shekel, the rate alone lowered for the poverty of the community

outliers.claim: Explains the shortage of Nethinim after the captivity by their status, since as descendants of the Gibeonites they were reckoned little better than slaves and had as much interest in staying in the land of their captivity as in returning.
Grounds the whole fund in the loss of the old temple treasures and the absence of a rich king such as Hezekiah, so that the charge fell on small yearly contributions from everyone.

themes: Also we made ordinances for us, to charge ourselves yearly with the third part of a shekel for the service of the house of our God;

For the shewbread, and for the continual meat offering, and for the continual burnt offering, of the sabbaths, of the new moons, for the set feasts, and for the holy things, and for the sin offerings to make an atonement for Israel, and for all the work of the house of our God.

35.pericope_label: And to bring the firstfruits of our ground, and the firstfruits of all fruit of all trees, year by year, unto the house of the Lord: Also the firstborn of our sons, and of our cattle, as it is written in the law, and the firstlings of our herds and of our flocks, to bring to the house of our God, unto the priests that minister in the house of our God: And that we should bring the firstfruits of our dough, and our offerings, and the fruit of all manner of trees, of wine and of oil, unto the priests, to the chambers of the house of our God; and the tithes of our ground unto the Levites, that the same Levites might have the tithes in all the cities of our tillage. And the priest the son of Aaron shall be with the Levites, when the Levites take tithes: and the Levites shall bring up the tithe of the tithes unto the house of our God, to the chambers, into the treasure house. For the children of Israel and the children of Levi shall bring the offering of the corn, of the new wine, and the oil, unto the chambers, where are the vessels of the sanctuary, and the priests that minister, and the porters, and the singers: and we will not forsake the house of our God.

schools.summary: Ellicott marks the change of construction at the head of the section, that the firstfruits follow on the ordinance made earlier rather than on the casting of lots, and infers from the minuteness of the specification that neglect had crept in, the Mosaic law having made this expression of natural piety an obligation. He observes that the sons stand collocated with the cattle as elsewhere in the law, where the cattle are expressly the unclean beasts, so that sons and unclean beasts alike were redeemed with money while the firstlings of herds and flocks went to the ministering priests for sacrifice; he explains that the priest had to be present when the Levites gathered tithes in the country in order to secure the priests' own portion, identifies the chambers as the store-chambers described in the account of the first temple with a treasure-house for tithes added later, and glosses the cities of tillage as the agricultural towns where produce was first deposited. On the closing pledge he notes drily that both the promise and its violation are explained by a later chapter of this same book. Keil and Delitzsch set out the whole scheme of firstfruits and firstborn, the ground and the fruit trees, the sons redeemed at the priest's valuation, the unclean cattle redeemed likewise, and the firstlings whose fat was consumed on the altar while the flesh fell to the priests; they note that the construction changes at this point from the infinitive to the first person, so that the undertaking passes from description into promise, and read the last clause as confirming what precedes.

Gill separates the firstfruits from the lot, holding that they were not settled by lot but undertaken by oath according to the law, and reports the narrower view of Aben Ezra restricting the term to the sheaf of the firstfruits and the two wave loaves. He identifies the cattle here meant as the unclean, the ass and its kind, and puts the check on the Levites in terms of motive rather than mechanism, that a priest was always present to observe the quantity received so that they might neither be tempted nor suspected.

Clarke supplies the reason behind the institution of the firstborn, that the Lord had a right to all of them and was pleased to take the tribe of Levi instead, so that the Levites served at the tabernacle and temple in the room of the firstborn of all the tribes. On the tithes he states the mechanism plainly, the tithes of all the produce going to the Levites and a tenth part of those to the priests, which is what the tithe of the tithes means. The closing pledge he takes as a text rather than a clause, building a whole scheme of the household of God upon it and ending by asking the reader whether he belongs to that house, whether he attends its ordinances, and whether he has forsaken it.

outliers.claim: Turns the closing pledge into a text, building from it a scheme of the house of God and its family and officers, and ending with direct questions to the reader about his own place in it.
Reads the pledge against what followed, noting that both the promise not to forsake the house of God and its breach are explained by a later chapter of this same book.
